title: What is Docker?
description: Understand containers, the Docker architecture, and how Docker differs from virtual machines.

data.text: A **container** is a lightweight, portable unit of software that packages an application and everything it needs to run — code, runtime, system tools, and libraries. Containers isolate applications from each other and from the host system, ensuring that the software runs consistently across any environment.

Containers solve the classic "it works on my machine" problem. Because the container bundles all dependencies, the application behaves the same way whether you are running it on a developer laptop, a staging server, or in production.

terms.definition: A read-only template used to create containers. An image includes the application code and all of its dependencies.
A runnable instance of an image — a lightweight, isolated process.
The core runtime that builds and runs containers using Docker. It consists of a daemon, a REST API, and a CLI.
A text file containing instructions for automatically building a Docker image.

data.text: Before containers, **virtual machines (VMs)** were the standard way to isolate workloads. Each VM includes a full guest operating system on top of a hypervisor. Containers are far more efficient because they share the host operating system kernel and only package the application layer.

cards.title: Containers
cards.description: Share host OS kernel; start in seconds; use less memory and disk.
pros: Higher density — many containers per host

cards.title: Virtual Machines
cards.description: Each VM bundles a full guest OS, offering stronger isolation.

data.caption: Docker architecture: you interact with the Docker CLI, which talks to the Docker daemon that manages images and containers.
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[Developer] -->|docker build / docker run| B[Docker CLI]
    B --> C[Docker Daemon/dockerd]
    C --> D[Image Cache]
    C --> E[Container Runtime]
    E --> F[Container]
    D --> F
    G[Container Registry] -.-> C

data.text: Containers have a clear lifecycle. You start with an image, create a container from it, run the container, and eventually stop and remove it. The image remains on disk and can be reused to start new containers.

items: **Build** — Create an image from a Dockerfile using `docker build`.
**Ship** — Push the image to a registry like Docker Hub using `docker push`.
**Run** — Start a container from the image using `docker run`.
**Stop** — Halt a running container with `docker stop`.
**Remove** — Delete a stopped container with `docker rm`.

data.title: Best practice
data.text: Use official base images from Docker Hub (like `node`, `python`, `nginx`) and always pin to a specific version tag to ensure reproducible builds.

items: **Docker daemon (dockerd)** — Runs in the background and manages images, containers, networks, and volumes.
**Docker CLI (docker)** — The command-line interface you type commands into.
**Docker Compose** — A tool for defining and running multi-container applications using a single YAML file.
**Docker Registry** — Stores and distributes Docker images (e.g., Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry).
**Docker API** — A REST API that programmatic tools can use instead of the CLI.

data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to describe the full Docker architecture and how its components work together.

data.title: Running your first container
data.content: Download the official Nginx image and run it. Then verify it's serving content.

data.title: What does the command do?
data.text: `-d` runs the container in the background (detached mode), `-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80, `--name webserver` gives the container a name, and `nginx:latest` is the image to use.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Containers package an application with all its dependencies for consistent behavior across environments.
Containers are more lightweight than VMs because they share the host OS kernel.
The Docker daemon manages images and containers; the CLI and API are the interfaces you use.
The container lifecycle is: build → ship → run → stop → remove.
data.takeaway: Docker makes applications portable and predictable — the foundation of modern DevOps.
